title: Minimax Estimation of Sparse Indirect Provider Ratios with a Rare Benchmark Event

proof_attempt_summary: The run proved matched all-sample ratio-MSE and common-width frontiers in its fixed known-scale, known-sparsity, external-pilot experiment; decision and math referees passed, and the three cited inequalities were attested. A calibrated parameter grid, precise source locators, and an explicit evaluable interval constant repaired the bounded findings, but the final cold novelty review still capped the package at subfield (7.3 versus the 7.4 field gate). Reaching field would require a re-anchored adaptive or same-sample result, or a new empirical component.
tldr: Indirect provider ratios compare each provider's observed binary outcome with the outcome expected for its own case mix. When the benchmark event is rare and the number of providers is large, fixed-dimensional efficient-influence-function theory does not reveal whether the ratio vector is estimable. The proposed theorem characterizes the all-sample weighted minimax risk as \(\frac{s}{k}\min\{1,\frac{k\log(ek/s)}{nb}+\delta^2\epsilon^2\}\). A clipped quotient of a total numerator and an orthogonal benchmark, followed by top-\(s\) retention, attains the rate. Paired rare-Bernoulli alternatives and collision-free common-outcome mixtures certify its sampling and nuisance components. Companion interval theorems give honest simultaneous coverage on samples with empty provider cells or zero events and a matched common-width frontier uniform over the stated confidence range.
gap: Published provider work identifies the indirect ratio and its efficient score, while published high-dimensional-treatment work controls sparse mean functionals and explicitly names indirect ratios as future work. Neither line gives the rare-event quotient information scale, a total random-denominator estimator, or legal lower bounds under a shared outcome regression and exact ratio sparsity.
fill: The project derives rare-score moments of order \(b/k\), stabilizes the quotient without a denominator good event, aggregates only the largest \(2s\) coordinate errors, and matches the resulting upper bound with ratio-compatible sampling and nuisance experiments. It also supplies honest all-provider intervals and separates their unresolved common-width converse.
